title: Recursive CTEs: requirement hierarchies and trace chains, with the CYCLE clause
summary: WITH RECURSIVE runs a start query, then repeats a step query on the rows the previous round produced until a round returns nothing: enough to walk requirement trees down and up, and trace graphs. SEARCH orders the result depth- or breadth-first, and CYCLE (PG 14) stops paths that revisit a node.

examples.title: A requirement tree: walking down with SEARCH DEPTH FIRST, and walking up

annotations.note: The non-recursive term runs once and produces the starting rows, here just AUTH at depth 0.
UNION ALL keeps every row. A tree has no duplicates to discard, so the cheaper ALL is right; graphs are another matter (example 2).

In each round, subtree stands for the rows the previous round produced, not everything so far. Round 1 finds AUTH's children, round 2 their children, round 3 finds nothing and the query stops. Each round joins on parent_id, so a real table wants an index on it.

SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY code (PG 14) adds a column, ord, that sorts every child right after its parent and siblings by code. Without it the rows come out breadth-first, which the docs call an implementation detail it is "perhaps unsound" to rely on.

Walking up is the same shape with the join reversed: each round finds the parent of the last row. It stops after AUTH, whose NULL parent_id matches nothing. The primary key index serves this direction.

examples.title: A trace graph with a cycle: the naive loop, CYCLE, and UNION

annotations.note: Without line 22 this query never ends: SYS-2 leads to SYS-3, SYS-3 back to SYS-2, and every lap produces rows that differ in hops. With the guard it ends at 6 hops, having reached SYS-2 three times and TC-10 four times. A depth limit bounds the damage; it doesn't detect the cycle.

CYCLE code SET is_cycle USING path adds two columns. path records the codes visited on the way to each row; when a step reaches a code already on its path, that row is emitted with is_cycle = true and not extended. Here SYS-2 at hop 3 closes the loop and the walk ends.
path is an array of row values, so ORDER BY path lists every route as a depth-first outline. TC-10 appears twice, once per route: in a graph, reachable through several paths is normal.

UNION discards rows that duplicate any earlier result row. With only the node itself in each row, a revisited node is a duplicate and the loop runs dry. Add hops or a path to the row and that protection is gone, which is why the CYCLE version needs CYCLE.

examples.title: Coverage per top-level requirement: carry the root down, then aggregate

annotations.note: Each round copies root_id from parent to child, so every requirement ends up tagged with its top-level ancestor. Anything derivable from the parent can be carried the same way: depth, a path, an inherited owner.

Test 10 is linked to AUTH-LOGIN and to AUTH-LOGIN-2FA, both inside AUTH's subtree: 4 links but 3 distinct tests. Rolling up over a hierarchy needs DISTINCT, or a test is counted once per requirement it covers.
FILTER from the GROUP BY lesson: failing tests per root, in the same pass as the totals.
LEFT JOINs keep EXPORT even though nothing below it has tests; its counts are 0, because count skips the NULL padding.

use_cases: Requirement and document hierarchies: everything under a requirement, the breadcrumb of ancestors, outlines in reading order
Traceability chains: from a stakeholder need through system requirements to the tests that verify it, and back
Org charts, category trees, threaded comments, bill-of-materials explosions
Impact analysis on dependency graphs: what is affected if this component changes
strengths: The whole walk is one query and one round trip, instead of one query per level from Go or TS
The tree stays a plain parent_id column with a foreign key, so writes are simple and integrity is enforced
SEARCH and CYCLE (PG 14) are standard SQL and replace hand-written path arrays and ANY() checks
Values can be carried down the walk (root, depth, path), so roll-ups need no second pass
weaknesses: UNION ALL over cyclic data never terminates; safety has to be written into every graph query
Each round is a join, so deep trees cost one join per level, and an unindexed parent_id means one table scan per level
Row order is undefined without SEARCH or an explicit ORDER BY on a path
Read-heavy, deep hierarchies can be cheaper with a materialized path (the ltree extension) or a closure table, at the cost of more complex writes

pitfalls.title: UNION ALL over a graph without a cycle check
pitfalls.detail: One bad link (A to B, B to A) makes the query run until a timeout or a resource limit stops it. Add CYCLE, or use UNION when each row is just the node.
pitfalls.bad: WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (SELECT 'STK-1'::text AS code, 0 AS hops UNION ALL SELECT l.to_code, r.hops + 1 FROM reach r JOIN trace_links l ON l.from_code = r.code) SELECT * FROM reach
pitfalls.good: WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (... same ...) CYCLE code SET is_cycle USING path SELECT * FROM reach

pitfalls.title: Expecting UNION to stop a walk that carries a depth
pitfalls.detail: UNION only drops rows that are entirely equal. (SYS-2, 1) and (SYS-2, 3) differ, so a cycle repeats forever. The docs make the same point for depth and path columns.

pitfalls.title: Relying on the output order
pitfalls.detail: Rows currently come out breadth-first, but the docs call that an implementation detail. Use SEARCH DEPTH FIRST or SEARCH BREADTH FIRST and ORDER BY the column it creates.

pitfalls.title: LIMIT as a loop guard
pitfalls.detail: A LIMIT in the outer query does stop runaway recursion in PostgreSQL, because only the rows fetched are computed. The docs recommend it for testing only: other systems might work differently.

pitfalls.title: Double counting in roll-ups
pitfalls.detail: A test linked to several requirements in one subtree is reached once per link. Count DISTINCT test ids, or deduplicate before aggregating.

quiz.q: During one round of the recursive term, what does the self-reference (subtree in example 1) contain?
options: Only the rows the previous round produced
quiz.why: The working table holds the previous round's new rows; each round's output replaces it, and the query stops when a round adds nothing.

quiz.q: The trace links contain a cycle. Which version is guaranteed to terminate?
options: UNION ALL with CYCLE code SET is_cycle USING path
quiz.why: Rows with a growing hops value are never equal, so neither UNION nor UNION ALL stops. CYCLE checks the code against the path and stops extending a path that revisits it.

quiz.q: Why does example 3 count DISTINCT test ids per root?
options: A test linked to two requirements in the same subtree would otherwise count twice
quiz.why: The walk reaches the test once per linked requirement. Distinct ids count each test once per root.

quiz.q: What does SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY code SET ord give you?
options: A column to ORDER BY so each child follows its parent, siblings by code
A guarantee that the CTE's output is already sorted
quiz.why: SEARCH only adds the ordering column; you still ORDER BY it. Cycle detection is CYCLE's job.

body:
## Concept

`WITH RECURSIVE` defines a CTE in two parts joined by `UNION ALL` (or `UNION`): a
**non-recursive term** that produces the starting rows, and a **recursive term** that
refers to the CTE itself. Despite the name, it is a loop, not recursion: the start rows
form the first round; each further round runs the recursive term against the previous
round's rows only; all rounds together are the result; the loop stops when a round
produces no rows.

That loop walks a **tree** stored as `parent_id`: down (children of the last round) or
up (the parent of the last row). It also walks a **graph**, such as trace links from
stakeholder needs through system requirements to test cases. Graphs bring two things
trees don't: a node reachable by several paths, and cycles. A cycle makes a `UNION ALL`
walk run forever.

PG 14 added two standard clauses after the CTE: `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST | BREADTH FIRST BY
col SET ordcol` adds a column to sort by, and `CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path` tracks
the path and stops extending a path when it revisits a node.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Any language:** this is the breadth-first frontier loop you have written many
  times: `frontier = [start]; while frontier: frontier = children_of(frontier);
  result += frontier`. The working table is `frontier`. `CYCLE` is a per-path `visited`
  check; `UNION` is a global `visited` set over whole rows.
- **Go and TS services:** without this, you either query once per level (N round trips)
  or load the whole table and build a `map[int][]int` of children in memory. The
  recursive CTE runs the loop next to the data and returns only the result.
- **Java/JPA:** a self-referencing `@OneToMany children` collection is lazy by default,
  so walking down issues one query per node whose children you touch. A native query
  with `WITH RECURSIVE` replaces the walk.
- **Python:** `networkx.descendants(G, 'STK-1')` returns the set of reachable nodes,
  which is what the `UNION` version of example 2 computes.

## How it works

Example 1, round by round:

1. Start: `AUTH` (depth 0).
2. Children of `AUTH`: `AUTH-LOGIN`, `AUTH-RESET` (depth 1).
3. Children of those: `AUTH-LOGIN-2FA`, `AUTH-LOGIN-LOCKOUT` (depth 2).
4. Children of those: none. Stop.

With `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL`, each round also drops rows equal to any row already
produced; that is what lets the node-only walk in example 2 terminate. `CYCLE` is
documented as a rewrite of a hand-written pattern: carry an array of visited keys,
mark a row whose key is already in it, and don't extend marked rows. `SEARCH` is a
similar rewrite that carries a sort key.

## Design notes

For hierarchies, start with an adjacency list (`parent_id REFERENCES` the same table)
and recursive CTEs: writes stay trivial, the foreign key keeps the tree honest, and
reads are one query. Index `parent_id` for downward walks. Consider a materialized path
(the `ltree` extension) or a closure table only when deep, read-heavy trees show up in
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`.

For graphs, make every traversal cycle-safe, even if the application is supposed to
prevent cycles: one bad link must not turn a page load into a timeout. Use `UNION` when
you need the set of reachable nodes, and `CYCLE` when you need paths, depths or
per-path data.

Carry what you need down the walk (root id, depth, path) and aggregate afterwards, and
remember that in a graph, or a roll-up over a tree with many-to-many links, the same
leaf arrives once per path: count distinct ids.

files.examples/01_tree.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.subqueries-ctes.recursive): the step query reruns on the last round's rows until none come back.
CREATE TABLE requirements (
  id        int PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_id int REFERENCES requirements,   -- NULL: a top-level requirement
  code      text NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO requirements VALUES
  (1, NULL, 'AUTH'), (2, 1, 'AUTH-LOGIN'), (3, 1, 'AUTH-RESET'),
  (4, 2, 'AUTH-LOGIN-2FA'), (5, 2, 'AUTH-LOGIN-LOCKOUT'),
  (6, NULL, 'EXPORT'), (7, 6, 'EXPORT-CSV');

-- Down the tree: AUTH and everything below it.
WITH RECURSIVE subtree AS (
  SELECT id, code, 0 AS depth              -- non-recursive term: the start
  FROM requirements
  WHERE code = 'AUTH'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.code, s.depth + 1         -- recursive term: children of
  FROM requirements c                      -- the rows found last round
  JOIN subtree s ON c.parent_id = s.id
) SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY code SET ord
SELECT repeat('. ', depth) || code AS outline, depth
FROM subtree
ORDER BY ord;

-- Up the tree: the ancestors of one leaf, nearest first.
WITH RECURSIVE ancestors AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, code, 0 AS up
  FROM requirements
  WHERE code = 'AUTH-LOGIN-2FA'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.id, p.parent_id, p.code, a.up + 1
  FROM requirements p
  JOIN ancestors a ON p.id = a.parent_id
)
SELECT up, code
FROM ancestors
ORDER BY up;
files.examples/02_trace_graph.sql:
-- Links from stakeholder needs (STK) to system requirements (SYS) to test
-- cases (TC) form a graph: TC-10 verifies two requirements, and a careless
-- link closes a loop (SYS-2 and SYS-3 point at each other).
CREATE TABLE trace_links (
  from_code text NOT NULL,
  to_code   text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (from_code, to_code)
);
INSERT INTO trace_links VALUES
  ('STK-1', 'SYS-1'), ('STK-1', 'SYS-2'),
  ('SYS-1', 'TC-10'), ('SYS-2', 'TC-10'), ('SYS-2', 'TC-11'),
  ('SYS-2', 'SYS-3'), ('SYS-3', 'SYS-2');

-- Naive: UNION ALL with no cycle check would never stop on this data.
-- A depth guard stops it, after the loop has repeated rows up to the guard.
WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (
  SELECT 'STK-1'::text AS code, 0 AS hops
  UNION ALL
  SELECT l.to_code, r.hops + 1
  FROM reach r
  JOIN trace_links l ON l.from_code = r.code
  WHERE r.hops < 6
)
SELECT code, count(*) AS times_reached
FROM reach
GROUP BY code
ORDER BY code;

-- CYCLE (PG 14) tracks the path and stops at a node already on it.
WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (
  SELECT 'STK-1'::text AS code, 0 AS hops
  UNION ALL
  SELECT l.to_code, r.hops + 1
  FROM reach r
  JOIN trace_links l ON l.from_code = r.code
) CYCLE code SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT hops, code, is_cycle, path
FROM reach
ORDER BY path;

-- Only need the set of reachable nodes? UNION discards rows it has already
-- produced, so the loop runs dry on its own.
WITH RECURSIVE reach(code) AS (
  SELECT 'STK-1'::text
  UNION
  SELECT l.to_code
  FROM reach r
  JOIN trace_links l ON l.from_code = r.code
)
SELECT code FROM reach ORDER BY code;
files.examples/03_rollup_coverage.sql:
CREATE TABLE requirements (
  id        int PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_id int REFERENCES requirements,
  code      text NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE test_cases (id int PRIMARY KEY, last_passed boolean NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE trace_links (
  requirement_id int REFERENCES requirements,
  test_case_id   int REFERENCES test_cases,
  PRIMARY KEY (requirement_id, test_case_id)
);
INSERT INTO requirements VALUES
  (1, NULL, 'AUTH'), (2, 1, 'AUTH-LOGIN'), (3, 1, 'AUTH-RESET'),
  (4, 2, 'AUTH-LOGIN-2FA'), (6, NULL, 'EXPORT'), (7, 6, 'EXPORT-CSV');
INSERT INTO test_cases VALUES (10, true), (11, false), (12, true);
-- Test 10 verifies two requirements in the same subtree.
INSERT INTO trace_links VALUES (2, 10), (4, 10), (4, 11), (3, 12);

-- Tag every requirement with its top-level ancestor by carrying the root's
-- id down the tree, then aggregate the linked tests per root.
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, id AS root_id FROM requirements WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, t.root_id
  FROM requirements c
  JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
)
SELECT root.code,
       count(l.test_case_id)          AS links,
       count(DISTINCT l.test_case_id) AS tests,
       count(DISTINCT l.test_case_id) FILTER (WHERE NOT tc.last_passed) AS failing
FROM tree
JOIN requirements root  ON root.id = tree.root_id
LEFT JOIN trace_links l ON l.requirement_id = tree.id
LEFT JOIN test_cases tc ON tc.id = l.test_case_id
GROUP BY root.id
ORDER BY root.code;
